<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Measuring Structured Predictability in Neural Training Dynamics: A Cross-Regime Study</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Fanqi Wang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Weisheng Tang
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Hairong Qi<span id="id1" class="ltx_ERROR undefined">\corresponding</span>
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern deep networks are trained through long update trajectories, yet their temporal organization remains less systematically characterized than architectures, losses, or optimizers. We study short-horizon predictability as a measure of temporal redundancy: where, when, and under which training conditions recent updates contain information about near-future parameter motion. We combine three complementary probe families—displacement-direction, subspace-residual, and predictor-based probes—with convention-aware, null-calibrated
group-level readouts, and apply them to multi-pass vision training on CIFAR and public Pythia pretraining checkpoints. Across both regimes,
vector-like tensors such as normalization parameters and biases (<em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">auxiliary parameters</em>) exhibit simpler short-horizon dynamics than matrix-like feature-transforming weights (<em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">bulk parameters</em>), whose predictable behavior concentrates in localized, time-varying pockets. Agreement within and across probe families, and with independent trajectory diagnostics, indicates that these measurements capture intrinsic trajectory structure, while probe differences distinguish complementary forms of temporal organization. Controlled CIFAR comparisons further show that architecture and training recipe systematically modulate the measured structure. A Pythia-70M case study further exposes a sequence of role-, depth-, and scale-dependent events, including bulk ESA falling below the random sign-agreement level and the emergence and redistribution of predictable <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="qkv" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">qkv</annotation></semantics></math> pockets across layers. These results position short-horizon predictability as a retrospective, parameter-resolved diagnostic of training dynamics.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center">Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, University of Tennessee, Knoxville</p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Modern neural networks are trained through long sequences of gradient evaluations and parameter updates, making iterative optimization a central computational bottleneck as models, datasets, and training horizons grow. A large body of work has studied architectures, losses, optimizers, final representations, gradient geometry, and loss-landscape structure
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gur-Ari et al. 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. 2018a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow et al. 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Draxler et al. 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Papyan et al. 2020</a>)</cite>.
In contrast, the temporal organization of the training trajectory remains less systematically characterized. Recent trajectory-level work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al. 2025</a>)</cite> has begun to characterize the global directional geometry of checkpoint paths, yet the short-horizon temporal redundancy of successive updates—the extent to which recent motion is informative about near-future displacement—has not been systematically characterized.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This gap is particularly relevant to predictive acceleration. Weight nowcasting, update extrapolation, predictive differential training, and related methods rely on recent history being informative about near-future parameter evolution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sinha et al. 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al. 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guan et al. 2024</a>)</cite>. Their success suggests that such information can exist, but not that it is uniform across parameters, training stages, architectures, or optimization recipes; indeed, Predictive Differential Training showed that selective prediction can be more reliable than prediction applied uniformly across a model. This motivates a more basic measurement question: <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where, when, and under what training conditions do neural update trajectories exhibit exploitable short-horizon structure?</em></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To answer this question, we develop three complementary probe families of increasing complexity. Displacement-direction probes test whether recent movement directions persist; subspace-residual probes ask whether future displacement remains within the span of recent updates; and predictor-based probes fit explicit local dynamics to capture richer temporal structure. We evaluate them at aggregate, tensor, and within-tensor group scales, with convention-aware and null-calibrated readouts for comparing localized structure under different grouping choices. Agreement and disagreement across the probes reveal shared and complementary forms of temporal organization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Across multi-pass vision training on CIFAR and one-pass pretraining of Pythia, the probes reveal a common spatial organization. Auxiliary, vector-like parameters exhibit simpler short-horizon dynamics than bulk, matrix-like parameters. Under the deepest probes considered here, bulk tensors are largely unpredictable in aggregate but contain localized subsets with elevated predictability whose identities shift over training. We call these localized, time-varying subsets <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">predictable pockets</em>. Beyond locating this structure, the probes reveal how it evolves with optimization. In controlled vision runs, directional readouts closely track movement directedness and gradient signal-to-noise ratio; ESA rapidly falls toward an anti-persistent floor, with later departures depending on parameter role and training condition.
In Pythia, temporal changes differ across QKV, attention-output, and MLP parameters and are not reducible to a single event in the scalar loss curve. More broadly, the short-horizon organization of training dynamics is jointly conditioned on optimization position, architecture, and training recipe; its parameter-resolved structure reveals where these differences are expressed within the model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, our contributions are:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a convention-aware, multiscale framework for measuring short-horizon temporal structure through three graded probe families: displacement-direction, subspace-residual, and predictor-based probes. The framework resolves aggregate, tensor, and within-tensor group structure, operates retrospectively on stored checkpoints, and provides a geometric ceiling for predictors constrained to the
recent-history span.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across multi-pass vision training and one-pass language-model pretraining, we identify a shared organization of predictability. Auxiliary and bulk parameters separate systematically in short-horizon dynamics, while bulk tensors contain localized, time-varying predictable pockets rather than uniformly predictable structure.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that the probe readings provide a state-sensitive, parameter-resolved view of optimization. They track realized movement structure, distinguish role-specific temporal events, and respond systematically to architecture and training recipe.
These results position short-horizon predictability as a retrospective diagnostic of temporal redundancy, distinct from optimizer quality and only conditionally relevant to predictive reuse.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work and Positioning</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Predicting future weights or updates has been explored as a way to accelerate neural training. Introspection learns weight-evolution patterns across runs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sinha et al. 2017</a>)</cite>; weight nowcasting and neuron-interaction nowcasting train auxiliary predictors to forecast near-future parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al. 2024</a>)</cite>; Predictive Differential Training uses Koopman/DMD-style forecasts with selective training-dynamics masks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. 2026</a>)</cite>; and optimizer-rule-based prediction has also been used to modify gradient-based training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guan et al. 2024</a>)</cite>. DMD and Koopman methods provide a natural linear-dynamical language for time-resolved trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmid 2010</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tu et al. 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dogra and Redman 2020</a>)</cite>. These works motivate the possibility of predictive training, but they are primarily predictor- or acceleration-centered. They do not systematically ask where short-horizon temporal regularity exists inside a model, whether it is localized or global, or how it changes with parameter role, training stage, architecture, optimizer, and training regime.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The closest work to ours studies the optimization trajectory as an object in its own right: <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Singh et al. (2025)</a></cite> show that the directional geometry of raw checkpoint paths saturates early at the macro level, oscillates at finer scales later, and is shaped in part by weight decay and momentum. We look at a different object. Rather than the path of the raw weights, we study the sequence of updates; rather than describing past geometry, we ask how well the recent past predicts the next few steps; and we answer at aggregate, tensor, and within-tensor scales. Existing trajectory-level studies characterize selected geometric properties of optimization paths, but a multiscale account of short-horizon parameter predictability spanning directional persistence, recent-history subspace structure, and explicit prediction remains missing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A separate body of work shows that neural training has rich structure. Gradients can align with low-dimensional Hessian subspaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gur-Ari et al. 2018</a>)</cite>, random-subspace experiments estimate intrinsic dimension <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. 2018a</a>)</cite>, and recent work questions whether such alignment identifies trainable projected subspaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. 2024</a>)</cite>. Loss-landscape studies reveal interpolation structure, mode connectivity, and useful weight averaging or ensembling along trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow et al. 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. 2018b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Draxler et al. 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garipov et al. 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Izmailov et al. 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al. 2022</a>)</cite>. Stage-wise analyses study edge-of-stability behavior, neural collapse, grokking, and lazy or kernel-like regimes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cohen et al. 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Papyan et al. 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Power et al. 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jacot et al. 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chizat et al. 2019</a>)</cite>.
These studies establish that optimization is structured, but they mainly concern spatial geometry, trainable subspaces, final representations, or named training regimes. Our object is the short-horizon temporal organization of parameter displacements, and where inside the model that structure resides.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">A further line of work uses pretraining suites with released intermediate checkpoints, most prominently Pythia <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al. 2023</a>)</cite>, to study how capabilities and circuits form along training, from the early emergence of induction heads <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olsson et al. 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tigges et al. 2024</a>)</cite> to compute-optimal accounts of over-training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoffmann et al. 2022</a>)</cite>. We use the Pythia checkpoints as our one-pass regime but measure something else: the temporal redundancy of the weight trajectory itself, not behaviors or circuits. When our readings line up in time with events reported in this literature, we note the correspondence and make no mechanistic claim.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Architecture and optimizer choices are also known to reshape optimization. Normalization, attention, and adaptive methods change Transformer optimization behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiong et al. 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. 2024</a>)</cite>; momentum, weight decay, sharpness-aware perturbations, slow–fast weight coupling, and matrix-structured updates alter the geometry of update sequences <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma and Ba 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Loshchilov and Hutter 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foret et al. 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma and Yarats 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jordan et al. 2024</a>)</cite>. Weight decay in particular has well-studied mechanisms, through its interaction with normalization and effective learning rates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">van Laarhoven 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">d’Angelo et al. 2024</a>)</cite>. Existing efficient-training methods reduce cost through pruning, sparse training, data selection, sample selection, or gradient and communication compression <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle and Carbin 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Evci et al. 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mirzasoleiman et al. 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Killamsetty et al. 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al. 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vogels et al. 2019</a>)</cite>. We take a complementary view: the optimizer trajectory itself may contain localized temporal redundancy. We therefore study short-horizon predictability as a trajectory-level measurement problem, rather than as an optimizer leaderboard or the performance of a single predictor, and we carry the same instruments across two training regimes — multi-pass vision training and one-pass language-model pretraining.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Measurement Framework</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We study short-horizon predictability as a property of a training trajectory rather than the performance of a single forecasting algorithm. Let <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the trainable parameters at checkpoint <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta w_{t}=w_{t+1}-w_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta w_{t}=w_{t+1}-w_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> the one-step update, and <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta w_{a}^{(\tau)}=w_{a+\tau}-w_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>a</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta w_{a}^{(\tau)}=w_{a+\tau}-w_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> the displacement realized over horizon <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> from anchor <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>. The preceding <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{past}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>past</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{past}}</annotation></semantics></math> updates form the local history <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{a}=[\Delta w_{a-n_{\mathrm{past}}},\ldots,\Delta w_{a-1}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>past</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{a}=[\Delta w_{a-n_{\mathrm{past}}},\ldots,\Delta w_{a-1}]</annotation></semantics></math>. Probes are evaluated on a measurement unit <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, either a whole trainable tensor or one of <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> disjoint within-tensor groups; <math id="S3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta w_{t,S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta w_{t,S}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{a,S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{a,S}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the corresponding restrictions. Every probe uses only history available before <math id="S3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and is evaluated retrospectively against the displacement after <math id="S3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>. Architectural roles are assigned only after measurement, for interpreting where predictable structure occurs. The choices of <math id="S3.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{past}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>past</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{past}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.p1.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, and grouping convention are specified with the experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use three complementary probe families of increasing representational complexity. <em id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Displacement-direction probes</em> test whether the latest update persists into the near-future displacement. <em id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Subspace-residual probes</em> ask whether that displacement remains within the low-dimensional span of recent updates, even when no single direction persists. <em id="S3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Predictor-based probes</em> test whether an explicit local model can exploit richer temporal structure. The families are therefore related but non-equivalent measurements of short-horizon organization.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Displacement-direction probes.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For element <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> of unit <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, let
<math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="e_{a,S,j}^{(\tau)}=\mathbf{1}\{\operatorname{sign}(\Delta w_{a-1,S,j})=\operatorname{sign}(\Delta w_{a,S,j}^{(\tau)})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>sign</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>sign</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e_{a,S,j}^{(\tau)}=\mathbf{1}\{\operatorname{sign}(\Delta w_{a-1,S,j})=\operatorname{sign}(\Delta w_{a,S,j}^{(\tau)})\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
<em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Element-wise sign agreement</em> (ESA) and <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">vector cosine similarity</em> (VCS) are</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">
<tbody>
<tr id="S3.E1X" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">ESA weights coordinates equally, whereas VCS weights them by displacement magnitude.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Subspace-residual probes.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{a,S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{a,S}</annotation></semantics></math> project onto the retained span of the recent-update matrix <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{a,S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{a,S}</annotation></semantics></math>. The <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">future residual ratio</em> (FRR) is</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{FRR}_{S}(a,\tau)=\frac{\|(I-P_{a,S})\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}\|_{2}}{\|\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}\|_{2}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>FRR</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{FRR}_{S}(a,\tau)=\frac{\|(I-P_{a,S})\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}\|_{2}}{\|\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}\|_{2}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where lower values indicate stronger containment in the recent-history span. An in-window control analogously evaluates the latest update against the span of the preceding <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{past}}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>past</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{past}}-1</annotation></semantics></math> updates. For groups <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{G_{g}\}_{g=1}^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>g</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{G_{g}\}_{g=1}^{K}</annotation></semantics></math>, the <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">low-residual group fraction</em> (LRGF) summarizes localization,</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathrm{LRGF}(a,\tau;\theta)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{g=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{FRR}_{G_{g}}(a,\tau)&lt;\theta\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>LRGF</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>K</mi></mfrac><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>K</mi></munderover><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>FRR</mi><msub><mi>G</mi><mi>g</mi></msub></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{LRGF}(a,\tau;\theta)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{g=1}^{K}\mathbf{1}\{\mathrm{FRR}_{G_{g}}(a,\tau)&lt;\theta\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Because the fixed threshold <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> is convention-dependent, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{LRGF}_{\rm cal}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>LRGF</mi><mi>cal</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{LRGF}_{\rm cal}</annotation></semantics></math> instead uses the <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.05</annotation></semantics></math> quantile of a size-matched permutation-null FRR distribution; under the null, its expected fraction is approximately <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, and we report excess over <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> where indicated.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Predictor-based probes.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A predictor maps the recent history to a predicted displacement <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{P},a,S}^{(\tau)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{P},a,S}^{(\tau)}</annotation></semantics></math>. We compare three increasingly expressive local models: inertia, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{in},a,S}^{(\tau)}=\tau\Delta w_{a-1,S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>in</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{in},a,S}^{(\tau)}=\tau\Delta w_{a-1,S}</annotation></semantics></math>; a per-element linear trend fitted to recent updates and integrated over the next <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> steps; and DMD, which fits and rolls forward a local linear map between consecutive update-history matrices. Because predicted magnitudes depend strongly on horizon and optimizer state, we emphasize direction and selection. The selector-free <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">predicted-direction cosine</em> is</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cos_{\mathrm{P},S}(a,\tau)=\frac{\langle\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{P},a,S}^{(\tau)},\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}\rangle}{\|\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{P},a,S}^{(\tau)}\|_{2}\,\|\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}\|_{2}},\quad\mathrm{P}\in\{\mathrm{in},\mathrm{lin},\mathrm{DMD}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>cos</mi><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>in</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>lin</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>DMD</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos_{\mathrm{P},S}(a,\tau)=\frac{\langle\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{P},a,S}^{(\tau)},\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}\rangle}{\|\widehat{f}_{\mathrm{P},a,S}^{(\tau)}\|_{2}\,\|\Delta w_{a,S}^{(\tau)}\|_{2}},\quad\mathrm{P}\in\{\mathrm{in},\mathrm{lin},\mathrm{DMD}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Since cosine ignores scale, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\cos_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv\mathrm{VCS}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>in</mi></msub><mo>≡</mo><mi>VCS</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv\mathrm{VCS}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Predictor outputs also define a selector
<math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="m_{a,S,j}=\mathbf{1}\{\operatorname{sign}(\widehat{f}_{a,S,j}^{(\tau)})=\operatorname{sign}(\Delta w_{a-1,S,j})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mi>sign</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>sign</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m_{a,S,j}=\mathbf{1}\{\operatorname{sign}(\widehat{f}_{a,S,j}^{(\tau)})=\operatorname{sign}(\Delta w_{a-1,S,j})\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">selected element-wise sign agreement</em> (SESA) and its <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">selectivity lift</em> over the unselected baseline are</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathrm{SESA}_{S}(m;a,\tau)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>SESA</mi><mi>S</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathrm{SESA}_{S}(m;a,\tau)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j\in S}m_{a,S,j}e_{a,S,j}^{(\tau)}}{\sum_{j\in S}m_{a,S,j}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j\in S}m_{a,S,j}e_{a,S,j}^{(\tau)}}{\sum_{j\in S}m_{a,S,j}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
